definition: To convince someone not to do something they were planning or considering.
example: Reports of heavy fog dissuaded the hikers from attempting the summit that morning.
nuance: Dissuade usually implies changing a mind through advice or argument, while deter often works through fear, cost or obstacles.
prompt: A friend wants to quit the school orchestra one week before its big concert.
options: Maya tried to dissuade her friend from quitting the orchestra so close to the concert.
Hoping he would leave, Maya tried to dissuade her friend by telling him to go right away.
The conductor dissuaded the orchestra through the final piece with a steady baton.
Maya dissuaded her friend from quitting, so he turned in his music folder that afternoon.
reasons: Trying to talk a friend out of a plan he is considering is exactly the right use.
Urging someone to carry out a plan pushes them toward it, which is the reverse.
Guiding musicians through a piece is leading them, not talking anyone out of a plan.
If he was talked out of quitting, he would stay rather than hand in his folder.

practice.prompt: A young cook is about to pour a whole cup of salt into a pot of soup.
options: To dissuade Leo, Grandpa handed him the salt and cheered while he poured it all in.
Grandpa dissuaded Leo that the soup needed more salt, so the boy added extra.
Leo dissuaded the soup with a wooden spoon until the noodles turned soft.
Grandpa managed to dissuade Leo from dumping a full cup of salt into the pot.
reasons: Cheering someone on encourages the plan instead of turning them away from it.
Convincing someone to add more is persuading, which points in the opposite direction.
Soup has no plans or intentions, so nobody can talk it out of anything.
Grandpa changes the boy's mind before he follows through on a bad idea.
